note.text:
A flowchart shows an algorithm as a diagram. Standard symbols:
• Oval (terminal): Start and Stop.
• Parallelogram: input or output.
• Rectangle: process (calculation, assignment).
• Diamond: decision (a yes/no question), with two exits.
• Arrows (flow lines): show the order of steps.
A loop is drawn as an arrow going back to an earlier step. Every flowchart has one Start and at least one Stop.

sections.heading: Algorithms as diagrams
sections.text:
A flowchart shows the steps of an algorithm with standard shapes joined by arrows. It makes the order of steps and the decisions easy to see.
• Oval (terminal): Start and Stop.
• Parallelogram: input or output (Read mark, Print result).
• Rectangle: process (total ← total + mark).
• Diamond: decision, a yes/no question with two exits.
• Arrows (flow lines): the order to follow.

sections.heading: Decisions and loops
sections.text:
A decision diamond asks a question such as 'Is mark ≥ {10}?'. One arrow leaves for Yes and another for No.
A loop is made by an arrow that goes back to an earlier step: for example, 'Is the PIN correct?' No → back to 'Input PIN'.
Make sure every loop can end, or the algorithm will run forever.

sections.heading: Reading a flowchart
sections.text:
Follow the arrows from Start with the given values, writing down each variable as it changes, until you reach Stop.
Start → Input L, W → A ← L × W → Output A → Stop. With L = {6} and W = {4}, the output is {24}.

key_words.meaning: a diagram of an algorithm using standard symbols
an arrow showing the order of steps

mistake.wrong: Using a rectangle for a yes/no question
mistake.right: Use a diamond for every decision
mistake.why: Diamonds have two exits for the two answers.

worked_example.problem: A flowchart: Start → Input L, W → A ← L × W → Output A → Stop. What is output when L = {l} and W = {w}?

cards.idea: Diamond = decision; rectangle = process; parallelogram = input/output; oval = start/stop.
Arrows show the order; an arrow going back makes a loop.
example: Repeat until a correct PIN is entered.

check.prompt: Flowchart: Start → Input n → Is n > {k}? Yes → n ← n − {d}, then go back to the question; No → Output n → Stop. What is output when n = {n}?

misconceptions.explain: The arrow goes back: keep subtracting while n > {k}.
{k} is never reached exactly here: list the values {n}, {n - d}, … until one is not greater than {k}.

solution: While n > {k}, subtract {d}: {n} goes down in steps of {d}.
The first value that is not greater than {k} is {k + r - d}.

cards.idea: A decision has two exits: Yes and No.

pick.y: A yes/no question is a decision.

e: It is not Start or Stop.
It is not Start or Stop.

pick.q: How many exits does a decision symbol have?
e: A decision chooses between two paths.
Only two answers to a yes/no question.

pick.r: by an arrow going back to an earlier step

pick.y: Terminals mark the beginning and end.

questions.prompt: Flowchart: Start → Input a, b → Is a > b? Yes → Output a; No → Output b → Stop. What is output when a = {a} and b = {b}?

misconceptions.explain: The Yes branch outputs a only when a is bigger; this flowchart outputs the larger number.

solution: So {answer} is output: the larger number.
